content: This is an updated version of a Cochrane Review originally published in 2018. Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological condition characterized by recurrent seizures. While most individuals with epilepsy respond well to a single antiepileptic drug, approximately 30% develop drug-resistant epilepsy, particularly those with focal seizures. This review evaluates the use of gabapentin as an add-on therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and tolerability of gabapentin when used as an adjunctive treatment in individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. For the latest update, a comprehensive search was conducted on August 11, 2020, using the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web) and MEDLINE (Ovid). The search included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials from multiple databases, with no language restrictions applied. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trials of gabapentin as an add-on therapy in individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Trials with active drug control groups or those comparing different doses of gabapentin were also included. Two independent reviewers selected the studies and extracted relevant data. The primary outcomes assessed were seizure frequency, seizure freedom, treatment withdrawal for any reason, and adverse effects. Analyses were conducted on an intention-to-treat basis, with additional sensitivity analyses performed. Summary risk ratios (RRs) were calculated for each outcome, and dose-response relationships were evaluated using regression models. No new studies were identified for this update, so the results and conclusions remain unchanged from the previous review. Data from six trials involving 1,206 randomized participants were included in the meta-analyses. The overall risk ratio (RR) for achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency with gabapentin compared to placebo was 1.89 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.40 to 2.55), based on moderate-certainty evidence. Dose-response analysis in adult trials demonstrated increased efficacy with higher doses of gabapentin. Specifically, 25.3% of participants responded to gabapentin at a dose of 1800 mg, compared to 9.7% on placebo, representing a 15.5% increase in response rate (95% CI 8.5 to 22.5). The RR for treatment withdrawal due to any reason was 1.05 (95% CI 0.74 to 1.49), based on moderate-certainty evidence. Adverse effects were more frequently associated with gabapentin compared to placebo. The RRs for specific adverse effects were as follows: ataxia (RR 2.01, 99% CI 0.98 to 4.11; low-certainty evidence), dizziness (RR 2.43, 99% CI 1.44 to 4.12; moderate-certainty evidence), fatigue (RR 1.95, 99% CI 0.99 to 3.82; low-certainty evidence), and somnolence (RR 1.93, 99% CI 1.22 to 3.06; moderate-certainty evidence). There was no significant difference in the incidence of headache (RR 0.79, 99% CI 0.46 to 1.35; moderate-certainty evidence) or nausea (RR 0.95, 99% CI 0.52 to 1.73; moderate-certainty evidence) between gabapentin and placebo groups. The studies included in this review were generally at low to unclear risk of bias, although some domains lacked sufficient information. The overall certainty of the evidence, assessed using the GRADE approach, was judged to be low to moderate due to potential attrition bias from missing outcome data and imprecise results with wide confidence intervals. In conclusion, gabapentin appears to be effective as an add-on treatment for individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and is relatively well-tolerated. However, the trials reviewed were of short duration, and there is no evidence supporting the long-term efficacy of gabapentin beyond three months. These findings cannot be generalized to monotherapy or to individuals with other types of epilepsy. Further research is needed to evaluate the long-term effects of gabapentin and to compare its efficacy and tolerability with other add-on antiepileptic drugs.
